catalog_locator: Ch. III, sec. 3.1.2.1 'Tone and the Stressed Syllable', pp. 65-66; sec. 3.1.2.5 'Summary of Analysis', item (1) Stress Placement, p. 74; exceptions p. 78; author's hedges p. 62 and p. 65
catalog_quote: Lexical pitch is associated with the stressed syllable in Gojri words (meaning Gojri is more like Swedish than Mandarin or other truly tonal languages where every syllable is tonally marked). The level tone occurs only on the stressed syllable. ... The assumption is that, within a morpheme, the location of stress can be predicted by syllable weight. ... Distinctions can therefore be made between light (where the rhyme consists of V), heavy (where the rhyme consists of VV or VC), and superheavy syllables (where the rhyme consists of VVC or VCC). ... If the final segment of a word is considered to be extra-metrical (not counted with respect to determination of syllable weight), then stress rules for Hindi-Urdu can be summarized as follows: the last heavy syllable in a word is stressed; if there is no heavy syllable (i.e. if the word consists of light syllables only), the penultimate syllable is stressed. These same stress assignment rules operate in Gojri. (pp. 65-66) ... (1) Stress Placement: - The last heavy syllable of the word is stressed; if there is no heavy syllable, the penultimate syllable is stressed; the last segment of the word is disregarded in the determination of syllable weight. - The causative suffix is always stressed; this fact overrides stress placement based on syllable structure. -There is only one stress per word, no matter whether the word is monomorphemic or morphologically complex. (p. 74)

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (283 pp., UND SIL Work Papers 46 reissue, text present; extracted text). All three quoted passages are at the stated locators, verbatim modulo line breaks. Printed p. 65 = p. 82, sec. 3.1.2.1 'Tone and the Stressed Syllable': "Lexical pitch is associated with the stressed syllable in Gojri words (meaning Gojri is more like Swedish than Mandarin or other truly tonal languages where every syllable is tonally marked). The level tone occurs only on the stressed syllable." Printed p. 66 continues: "the last heavy syllable in a word is stressed; if there is no heavy syllable.. the penultimate syllable is stressed. These same stress assignment rules operate in Gojri. For example, the word /…
new_statements.rule_in_words: With the word-final segment treated as extrametrical, stress falls on the last heavy syllable (rhyme VV or VC after extrametricality); if the word has only light syllables, stress is penultimate (so /'jisam/ 'body', /as'maːN/ 'sky'). Morphology can override: the causative suffix is always stressed. Gojri also has lexical tone (level, high-falling, low-rising), whose pitch targets are anchored on the stressed syllable — Losey compares it to Swedish rather than Mandarin.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the summary states there is only one stress per word.
new_statements.exceptions: Causative suffix always stressed (morphological override of weight). p. 78: 'For a small number of words, stress falls on a non-initial syllable', e.g. /daːde'aːL/ 'paternal relatives', /male'ap/ 'worm', for which 'it is not clear why stress and the low-rising tone occur on the short-vowel ultima.' Losey adds that the rule is taken over from Hindi-Urdu stress studies (Dyrud 2001, Hussain 1997) as an assumption that the location of stress is predictable from syllable weight, and that a complete analysis of Gojri prosody had not yet been undertaken (p. 62).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical stress in phonemic transcriptions of words from Kaghan and Allai word lists (citation forms); data are the Kaghani Bakarwal ('Eastern') and Allaiwal Bakarwal ('Western') Gojri of Hazara, Pakistan, collected 1999-2001.
new_statements.identity_note: Losey 2002 describes the Gojri of Bakarwal (transhumant) Gujars of Hazara, Pakistan: Kaghani Bakarwal (his 'Eastern' dialect type, Kaghan Valley) and Allaiwal Bakarwal (his 'Western' dialect type, Allai); he compares them with Sharma's Punch (Poonch, J&K, India) Gojri. Glottolog guja1253 has no dialect subdivisions; both fall under guja1253 (ISO gju). Sharma 1982 (Poonch Gojri) describes three tones and is silent on stress.

sources.note: Ch. I Phonology pp. 10-59 lists segmentals plus suprasegmental phonemes = three tones: 'Tones: There are three tones. Low tone marked by /\/, High tone marked by /^/, Mid tone is unmarked.' (p. 12; p. 27, image), tone contrasts p. 24 ff., junctures pp. 54-56, syllable structure p. 56. No statement about stress or accent anywhere (full scanned text a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence). Data: Poonch district, J&K, India, 1973-75.
Mentions a high tone and nasalization; nothing on stress; bibliography pointed to Losey 2002 and Bashir 2016.
